$$ v^{0}=\frac{\p\phi^{0}}{\p x},\quad b^{0}=\frac{\p\phi^{0}}{\p z},\quad u^{1}=\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p z},\quad w^{1}=-\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p x}. $$

With the forcing terms $F_{v}$ and $F_{b}$ given by

$$ \displaystyle F_{v} \displaystyle=-\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{S}\frac{\p\phi^{0}}{\p x}+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{HV}\frac{\p}{\p x}\left(\nu_{H}\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x^{2}}\right)+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{VV}\frac{\p}{\p z}\left(\nu_{V}\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\right)+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{S}x\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x^{2}}, \displaystyle F_{b} \displaystyle=\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{HD}\frac{\p}{\p x}\left(\kappa_{H}\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\right)+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{VD}\frac{\p}{\p z}\left(\kappa_{V}\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p z^{2}}\right)+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{S}x\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}, $$

pressure is given by the hydrostatic relationship to obtain a system for $(\psi^{1},v^{1},b^{1})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\textit{Ro}}\frac{\p}{\p t}\left(\frac{\p^{2}\psi^{1}}{\p z^{2}}\right)-\frac{\p v^{1}}{\p z}+\frac{\p b^{1}}{\p x} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\frac{\p v^{1}}{\p t}+\left(\frac{1}{\textit{Ro}}+{\textit{Ro}}\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x^{2}}\right)\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p z}-{\textit{Ro}}\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p x} \displaystyle={F}_{v}(x,z;\phi^{0}), \displaystyle\frac{\p b^{1}}{\p t}+{\textit{Ro}}\left(\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p z}-\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p z^{2}}\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p x}\right) \displaystyle={F}_{b}(x,z;\phi^{0}), $$

We further reduce the system to a single equation for $\psi^{1}$ as

$$ \frac{1}{\textit{Ro}}\frac{\p^{4}\psi^{1}}{\p t^{2}\p z^{2}}+{\textit{Ro}}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\textit{Ro}^{2}}+\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x^{2}}\right)\frac{\p^{2}\psi^{1}}{\p z^{2}}-2\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\frac{\p^{2}\psi^{1}}{\p x\p z}+\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p z^{2}}\frac{\p^{2}\psi^{1}}{\p x^{2}}\right]=\frac{\p F_{v}}{\p z}-\frac{\p F_{b}}{\p x}. $$

This governing equation for the streamfunction perturbation $\psi^{1}(x,z,t)$ is a linear, inhomogeneous partial differential equation. Substituting the coefficients derived from $v^{0}$ and $b^{0}$ for $\phi^{0}$ , the equation takes the form

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial^{2}\psi^{1}}{\partial z^{2}}\right)+J_{0}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial z}-\textit{Ro}^{2}\,B^{\prime}_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\right)^{2}\psi^{1}=F_{1}(x,z)\equiv\textit{Ro}\,\left(\frac{\p F_{v}}{\p z}-\frac{\p F_{b}}{\p x}\right), $$

The solution is sought subject to the boundary conditions $\psi^{1}(z=0,1)=0$ and initial conditions $\psi^{1}(t=0)=0$ and $\psi^{1}_{t}(t=0)=0$ .

The most direct method of solution is to employ superposition, decomposing the streamfunction into a time-independent particular solution, $\psi^{1}_{p}(x,z)$ , and a time-dependent homogeneous solution, $\psi^{1}_{h}(x,z,t)$ :

$$ \psi^{1}(x,z,t)=\psi^{1}_{p}(x,z)+\psi^{1}_{h}(x,z,t). $$

The particular solution $\psi^{1}_{p}$ satisfies the steady-state equation, balancing the background forcing:

$$ J_{0}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial z}-\textit{Ro}^{2}\,B^{\prime}_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\right)^{2}\psi^{1}_{p}=F_{1}(x,z). $$

This equation is simplified by a change of coordinates from $(x,z)$ to $(X_{0},Z)$ . In this new frame, the advective derivative operator becomes $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}-\textit{Ro}^{2}\,B^{\prime}_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial Z}$ , and the spatial derivative transforms as $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}=J_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial X}$ . Applying this transformation to (26) yields

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}\tilde{\psi}^{1}_{p}}{\partial Z^{2}}=J_{0}^{-1}F_{1}(X_{0},Z), $$

where tildes denote functions in the $(X_{0},Z)$ coordinate system. Equation (27) is an ordinary differential equation for $\tilde{\psi}^{1}_{p}(X_{0},Z)$ in the variable $Z$ , with $X_{0}$ treated as a parameter. We solve (27) by direct integration:

$$ \tilde{\psi}^{1}_{p}(X_{0},Z)=\int_{0}^{Z}\int_{0}^{Z^{\prime}}J_{0}^{-1}F_{1}(X_{0},Z^{\prime\prime})\,\mathrm{d}Z^{\prime\prime}\,\mathrm{d}Z^{\prime}+C_{1}(X_{0})Z+C_{2}(X_{0}). $$

The functions $C_{1}(X_{0})$ and $C_{2}(X_{0})$ are determined by the boundary conditions $\tilde{\psi}^{1}_{p}(X_{0},0)=0$ and $\tilde{\psi}^{1}_{p}(X_{0},1)=0$ , yielding $C_{2}(X_{0})=0$ and $C_{1}(X_{0})=-\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{Z^{\prime}}J_{0}^{-1}F_{1}(X_{0},Z^{\prime\prime})\,\mathrm{d}Z^{\prime\prime}\,\mathrm{d}Z^{\prime}$ . This procedure fully specifies the particular solution $\psi^{1}_{p}$ .

The homogeneous solution $\psi^{1}_{h}$ satisfies the unforced equation

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial^{2}\psi^{1}_{h}}{\partial z^{2}}\right)+J_{0}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial z}-\textit{Ro}^{2}\,B^{\prime}_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\right)^{2}\psi^{1}_{h}=0, $$

with homogeneous boundary conditions and modified initial conditions derived from the total solution:

$$ \psi^{1}_{h}(t=0)=-\psi^{1}_{p}(x,z),\quad\frac{\partial\psi^{1}_{h}}{\partial t}(t=0)=0. $$

We solve (29) via a normal mode analysis, seeking solutions of the form $\psi^{1}_{h}(x,z,t)=\text{Re}[\hat{\psi}^{1}(x,z)e^{-i\omega t}]$ . This leads to a generalized eigenvalue problem for the spatial mode structure $\hat{\psi}^{1}$ and the frequency $\omega$ :

$$ \mathcal{L}[\hat{\psi}^{1}]\equiv J_{0}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial z}-\textit{Ro}^{2}\,B^{\prime}_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\right)^{2}\hat{\psi}^{1}=\omega^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}\hat{\psi}^{1}}{\partial z^{2}}. $$

Solving (31) provides a set of eigenfunctions $\hat{\psi}^{1}_{n}$ and corresponding eigenfrequencies $\omega_{n}$ . The general homogeneous solution is a linear combination of these modes. Given the initial condition $\psi^{1}_{h,t}(t=0)=0$ , the solution simplifies to a cosine series:

$$ \psi^{1}_{h}(x,z,t)=\sum_{n}A_{n}\cos(\omega_{n}t)\hat{\psi}^{1}_{n}(x,z). $$

The coefficients $A_{n}$ are found by projecting the initial condition $-\psi^{1}_{p}$ onto the eigenbasis:

$$ \sum_{n}A_{n}\hat{\psi}^{1}_{n}(x,z)=-\psi^{1}_{p}(x,z). $$

Assuming the eigenfunctions form a complete set, orthogonal under an appropriate inner product, the coefficients $A_{n}$ are uniquely determined. Dynamically, the unforced first-order solution with a zeroth-order geostrophic balance is equivalent to the evolution of a balanced state under perturbed higher-order imbalance. And this leads to the geostrophic adjustment solution in ST13. Therefore, we argue that the homogeneous solution is dominated at the inertial frequency $\omega=1$ so that $\psi^{1}_{h}(x,z,t)\approx-\psi^{1}_{p}(x,z)\cos{t}$ . Although this is not an exact solution of (29), we demonstrate later that it only has higher-order errors near boundaries and large gradients, so this approximation is consistent with the perturbation analysis.

The final solution is then the sum $\psi^{1}=\psi^{1}_{p}+\psi^{1}_{h}$ , which can be approximated as $\psi^{1}\approx(1-\cos{t})\psi^{1}_{p}$ , assuming the homogeneous component is dominated by near-inertial modes. Given $\psi^{1}\approx(1-\cos{t})\psi^{1}_{p}$ , the corresponding solutions for $v^{1}$ and $b^{1}$ are then

$$ \displaystyle{v^{1}} \displaystyle\approx{F}_{v}(x,z;\phi^{0})t-\textit{Ro}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\textit{Ro}^{2}}+\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x^{2}}\right)\frac{\p\psi^{1}_{p}}{\p z}-\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\frac{\p\psi^{1}_{p}}{\p x}\right]\left(t-\sin{t}\right), \displaystyle{b^{1}} \displaystyle\approx{F}_{b}(x,z;\phi^{0})t-\textit{Ro}\left(\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\frac{\p\psi_{p}^{1}}{\p z}-\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p z^{2}}\frac{\p\psi_{p}^{1}}{\p x}\right)\left(t-\sin{t}\right). $$

We note that the time dependence in the first order system consists of a linear and sinusoidal part. This defers from the classic frontogenesis case as it does not include an exponential term. Another useful diagnostic measure for frontal tendency is the Lagrangian evolution of the horizontal buoyancy gradient (Bodner et al., 2019)

$$ T_{b}=\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{D}t}\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\p b}{\p x}\right)^{2}=T_{b}^{0}+\epsilon T_{b}^{1}+\textit{O}(\epsilon^{2}), $$

with $T_{b}^{0}=0$ due to zeroth-order geostrophic balance and

$$ T_{b}^{1}=\frac{1}{\textit{Ro}}\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\frac{\p^{2}b^{1}}{\p t\p x}+\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p z}-\frac{\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{S}}{\textit{Ro}}x\right)\frac{\p}{\p x}-\frac{\p\psi^{1}}{\p x}\frac{\p}{\p z}\right]\left(\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\right)^{2}, $$

which consists of a constant and sinusoidal parts. Therefore, the first-order model describes a quasi-linear frontal strengthening or weakening under comparable strain and BLT perturbations. In particular, as we split $F_{1}$ into different mechanisms as

$$ F_{1}=F_{S}+F_{HV}+F_{VV}+F_{HD}+F_{VD}, $$

which consists of contributions from strain ( $F_{S}$ ) and BLT ( $F_{HV},F_{VV},F_{HD},F_{VD}$ ). We first examine them separately and then explore their combined effect.

### 4.2 First-order solution: strain-only

In the strain-only case, we set ${\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{S}}=1$ and all BLT terms to zero, giving

$$ F_{S}={\textit{Ro}}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(-\frac{\p\phi^{0}}{\p x}+x\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x^{2}}\right)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(x\frac{\p^{2}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z}\right)\right]=-2{\textit{Ro}}B^{\prime}_{0}J_{0}, $$

and the corresponding particular solution is

$$ \psi^{1}_{p,S}=-\textit{Ro}\,{B_{0}^{\prime}(X_{0})}Z(Z-1). $$

We can obtain an approximate full solution with $\psi^{1}_{S}\approx(1-\cos{T})\psi^{1}_{p,S}$ . The first-order velocity and buoyancy can be derived from $\psi^{1}_{S}$ as

$$ \displaystyle v^{1}_{S} \displaystyle=\left(Z-\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{T[B^{\prime\prime}_{0}(X_{0})X_{0}+B^{\prime}_{0}(X_{0})]-2{B^{\prime}_{0}(X_{0})}\sin{T}}{1-\textit{Ro}^{2}\,B^{\prime\prime}_{0}(X_{0})(Z-\frac{1}{2})}, \displaystyle b^{1}_{S} \displaystyle={B^{\prime}_{0}(X_{0})}(TX_{0}+\textit{Ro}^{2}\,v^{1}_{S}). $$

We show the derivation details, comparison with ST13, and analysis of the approximation accuracy in Appendix 7.

### 4.3 First-order solution induced by boundary-layer turbulence

For simplicity, we here assume $\textit{Ro}=1$ with constant viscosities and diffusivities. Yet note that the analysis can be applied to more generalized cases. Assuming $\Pran_{V}<1$ , $\Pran_{H}<1$ and $\nu_{V}=\nu_{H}=\kappa_{V}=\kappa_{H}=1$ after dimensionless normalization, typical of BLT in the mixed layer (Sullivan and McWilliams, 2018, e.g.,), the effect of BLT on $\psi^{1}$ comes from the vertical and horizontal diffusion fluxes as

$$ F_{VD}\propto-\frac{\p^{4}\phi^{0}}{\p x\p z^{3}},\quad F_{VV}\propto-F_{VD},\quad F_{HD}\propto-\frac{\p^{4}\phi^{0}}{\p x^{3}\p z},\quad F_{HV}\propto-F_{HD}, $$

which arrives from combining (20) with the definition of $F_{1}$ in (24) for each case.

To isolate the respective effects of horizontal and vertical diffusivity and viscosity, we fix the corresponding forcing parameters to $\varepsilon_{i}=0.03$ , an average of a realistic estimate in Appendix 6, with $i\in\{HV,VV,HD,VD\}$ while keeping all others as zero. We discuss a larger parameter exploration in the following section and compare it with strain. Figures 4 and 5 illustrate the resulting velocity, buoyancy, and frontal tendency structures at $t=10$ .

The vertical diffusivity has a negligible impact on the along-front velocity structure for both the front and filament cases. However, the frontal tendency reveals weak frontolysis in the interior and frontogenesis near the outer isopycnals, structurally similar to the strain-driven cases (figures 4a,b and 5a,b). In contrast, vertical viscosity introduces significant vertical shear, skewing the velocity distribution such that the maximum shifts toward the frontal edges and spreads vertically. This effect is particularly pronounced in the filament case, where the center near-surface velocity is strengthened (figure 4c,d). The corresponding frontal tendency exhibits an asymmetric dipole pattern across isopycnals, which is mirrored across $x=0$ for the filament (figure 5c,d).

In the horizontal diffusivity regime, the velocity profile remains largely robust in the frontal case, whereas the buoyancy contours exhibit significant broadening (figure 4e). This diffusive widening is most evident in the filament case, where the central isopycnals are heavily distorted near $x=0$ , indicating effective erosion of the filament buoyancy gradient (figure 4f). This is confirmed by the frontal tendency analysis, which shows the strongest and spatially widest frontolytic signature among all cases (figure 5e,f). For horizontal viscosity, the velocity structure undergoes a bimodal splitting along the horizontal boundaries (figure 4g), evolving into a quad-modal structure near the surface in the filament case (figure 5h). The associated frontal tendency resembles that of the vertical viscosity case but is spatially broader, characterized by enhanced frontogenesis at the surface and frontolysis at depth (figure 5g,h). In this case, the first-order solution is likely being comparable to the zeroth-order solution, such that the perturbation assumption become less accurate at $t=10$ .

*Figure 6: Evolution of the front width under various turbulent forcing terms for (a) front and (b) filament. The relevant parameter is set to $\varepsilon_{i}=0.03$ with $i\in\{HV,VV,HD,VD\}$ and $\textit{Ro}=1$ .*

Figure 6 illustrates the temporal evolution of the frontal width under these distinct turbulent regimes. In the case of vertical diffusivity, the width remains quasi-steady, exhibiting minor oscillations consistent with the balance between competing frontogenetic and frontolytic tendencies. Conversely, vertical viscosity induces a transient widening followed by a gradual contraction, a behavior likely governed by the complex spatial interplay of the tendency terms. The most notable evolution occurs under horizontal diffusivity: the front initially widens significantly, peaking at $t\approx 10$ for the front and slightly earlier for the filament, before undergoing a rapid contraction. This reversal is particularly pronounced in the filament case, where the width collapses to its minimum value in all cases by $t=15$ (figure 6b). This non-monotonic behavior suggests that while diffusion initially spreads the front, the eventual dominance of frontolysis promotes the emergence of new internal buoyancy gradients, effectively re-sharpening the feature and likely making the perturbation limit less accurate. Finally, horizontal viscosity leads to a monotonic reduction in width over time, aligning with the broadly expanded frontogenetic pattern previously identified. The divergence in these evolutionary pathways suggests that the compound effects of boundary layer turbulence yield a highly dynamic and complex frontal response.

Previous studies have established that vertical mixing, comprising both diffusivity and viscosity, can either induce or inhibit submesoscale frontogenesis (Dauhajre et al., 2025). We investigate this phenomenon using our first-order model under constant coefficients, yet we do not observe a similar transition (figure 8a). Therefore, in the asymptotic setting, the transition is likely sensitive to spatial variabilities of turbulence coefficients or higher-order effects (Dauhajre et al., 2025).

### 4.4 Competition between strain and boundary-layer turbulence

*Figure 7: Evolution of strain-induced frontogenesis under various turbulent forcing terms for front (left column) and filament (right column) with $\textit{Ro}=1$ . Shown are time series with (a,b) vertical diffusivity, (c,d) vertical viscosity, (e,f) horizontal diffusivity, and (g,h) horizontal viscosity. The strain-only case is in black, and dark to light blues denote an increase of the turbulent scale $\varepsilon$ as $1/3\varepsilon_{S},\varepsilon_{S},5/3\varepsilon_{S},7/3\varepsilon_{S},3\varepsilon_{S}$ with $\varepsilon_{S}=0.03$ .*

Since perturbations arising from mesoscale strain and boundary-layer turbulence (BLT) frequently coexist, we investigate the frontal response to their concurrent forcing. We initially fix the strain parameter at $\gamma=\varepsilon_{S}=0.03$ , equal to the average BLT parameter used previously, and vary the magnitude of the BLT fluxes (figure 7). Later we also present results for a wider range of strain values. For each BLT component, the respective perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$ is increased from 0 up to $3\varepsilon_{S}$ . Horizontal diffusivity exerts the strongest modulation on the frontogenetic process, whereas other fluxes serve to either enhance or mitigate frontal sharpening depending on the temporal phase and the specific frontal configuration.

Specifically, vertical diffusivity introduces inertial oscillations to the strain-induced frontogenesis. In the frontal configuration, this results in a marginally reduced rate of sharpening (figure 7a). Conversely, for the filament, vertical diffusivity consistently enhances sharpening for $t>3$ , despite an initial period of broadening similar to the frontal case (figure 7b). This likely stems from the structural alignment between the frontal tendency patterns induced by strain and those induced by vertical diffusivity in the filament geometry (cf. figure 5b). Vertical viscosity, however, consistently inhibits filament sharpening. For the front, moderate viscosity scales lead to widening, while the largest magnitude ( $\varepsilon=3\varepsilon_{S}$ ) induces sharpening after $t\approx 10$ . This suggests that the bimodal surface tendency patterns associated with vertical viscosity generally counteract strain-driven frontogenesis, although extreme viscous forcing can eventually dominate the dynamics to favor frontogenesis (figure 5c,d).

Horizontal diffusivity is unique in its ability to trigger transient frontolysis even in the presence of strain (figure 7e,f). For the front, a diffusivity scale of $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{S}/3$ significantly weakens sharpening, while $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{S}$ yields a quasi-steady width, and stronger diffusion ( $\varepsilon>\varepsilon_{S}$ ) leads to broadening over finite times (figure 7e). The filament case exhibits similar but more pronounced behavior; notably, at later times, strong horizontal diffusivity can trigger sharper widths than the strain-only reference case (figure 7f). Finally, horizontal viscosity demonstrates a weak mitigating effect at small magnitudes but becomes dominantly frontogenetic at large magnitudes, a trend that is consistent across both front and filament configurations (figure 7g,h).

We calculate the frontogenesis metric $1/d$ at $t=10$ (approximately 1.5 inertial periods), following Dauhajre et al. (2025).

In the absence of strain ( $\varepsilon_{S}=0$ ), the $1/d$ values remain largely at unity across the parameter space for both configurations, corresponding to lack of frontogenesis (figure 8a,b). Exceptions appear at $(\textit{Ro},\textit{Ek}_{V})=(1.6,10^{-1})$ for front and $(1.6,10^{-1}),(1.6,10^{-2}),(1.0,10^{-1})$ for filament, which shows frontogenetic levels significantly higher than unity. Under weak strain ( $\varepsilon_{S}=0.025$ ), the reference inviscid cases ( $\textit{Ek}_{V}=0$ ) exhibit comparably low levels of frontogenesis across all Rossby numbers (figure 8c,d). The inclusion of vertical mixing generally results in values overlapping with these background levels, excepting super-frontogenetic outliers $(\textit{Ro},\textit{Ek}_{V})$ combinations same as those in the zero-strain case. However, the tendency is significantly weakened for the front scenario at $(\textit{Ro},\textit{Ek}_{V})=(1.0,10^{-1}),(1.6,10^{-2})$ .

As the strain increases to moderate levels ( $\varepsilon_{S}=0.05$ ), the inviscid reference levels become distinctly stratified by Rossby number, with higher Ro yielding stronger frontogenesis (figure 8e,f). The previously identified deviations persist but with altered relative magnitudes; for instance, the front at $\textit{Ro}=1.0,\textit{Ek}_{V}=10^{-1}$ remains the most inhibited case, while cases at $\textit{Ek}_{V}=10^{-2}$ show similar frontogenetic levels. Under strong strain ( $\varepsilon_{S}=0.1$ ), the stratification of the inviscid reference levels is further amplified (figure 8g,h). In this regime, higher Ro gives stronger frontogenesis for frontal cases at $\textit{Ek}_{V}=10^{-2}$ , although its values at $\textit{Ro}=1.6$ remains substantially weakened than the baseline. That said, a step-like pattern start to emerge in the frontal case, while other patterns remain similar to those under moderate strain. If we compare the results to the viscosity-only case with $\Pran_{V}=\infty$ , as explored in Dauhajre et al. (2025), the frontogenetic strength are generally stronger when diffusivity is present, except at $\textit{Ro}=1.0,\textit{Ek}_{V}=10^{-1}$ (figure 15). Therefore, in this framework the weak-strong frontogenesis division is governed by the Ro-sensitive strain effect, in contrast to the diffusivity-viscosity competition discussed in Dauhajre et al. (2025) which neglects strain.

These results underscore the complex, non-monotonic interplay between strain-driven frontogenesis and vertical mixing, revealing a high sensitivity to the specific dynamical regime defined by the Rossby and Ekman numbers. And based on the analysis under a fixed strain and varied degrees of each BLT flux (figure 7), we expect more sophisticated interactions once horizontal mixing is also considered. Here we demonstrate this by setting $\textit{Ek}=\textit{Ek}_{V}=\textit{Ek}_{H}$ with $\Pran_{V}=\Pran_{H}=1$ and repeat the Ro–Ek parameter space exploration as done in figure 8, so all terms of horizontal and vertical viscosity and diffusivity are present at equal magnitudes. As expected, the results show a more robust step-like transition for both front and filament, and the frontogenetic level $1/d$ can drop below unity. However, if we consider only viscosities by setting $\Pran_{V}=\Pran_{H}=\infty$ , the frontolytic cases with $1/d$ significantly below unity disappear (figure 16). Therefore, in this case certain frontolytic-frontogenetic dynamic partitions similar to that in Dauhajre et al. (2025) are emerging (figure 9), yet the difference of adding horizontal mixing illustrate the effect of $\textit{Ek}_{H}$ , and the difference of removing diffusivities implies that horizontal diffusivity dominates the frontolytic evolution than any other terms. Therefore, horizontal mixing is critical in this perturbation model for frontolytic evolution, as suggested already in B19.

## 5 Discussion and conclusions

In this study, we have performed a perturbation analysis of initially geostrophically balanced 2D fronts and filaments subject to comparable mesoscale strain and boundary layer turbulence (BLT), a regime typical of weakly stratified oceanic mixed layers. The initial configuration adapts the analytical solution of Shakespeare and Taylor (2013), assuming zero PV and a finite Rossby number typical of submesoscale dynamics. This approach complements the semi-geostrophic analysis of Bodner et al. (2019) (hereafter B19), enabling a systematic examination of frontal characteristics across a broad range of Rossby, Ekman, and normalized strain numbers. We note that while some submesoscale fronts can extend below the mixed layer (Siegelman et al., 2020), our analysis is confined to the mixed-layer alone.

When both strain and BLT are treated as perturbations, we assume the zeroth-order solution as a geostrophic balance that permits finite Rossby numbers. The first-order perturbation solution is substantially simplified by initializing the zeroth-order state in geostrophic balance. This allows the system to be reduced to one involving only the first-order cross-front streamfunction, which we solve using momentum-following coordinates and normal-mode analysis. For pure strain perturbations, our solution is closely related to that of Shakespeare and Taylor (2013); indeed, treating the strain parameter as a perturbation in their analysis would yield a matching result, albeit with a non-exponential but persistent frontal tendency. In the early inertial period, these approximations show strong agreement. In the real ocean, the effect of BLT can be comparable to and limit strain-induced frontogenesis, in which case the linear perturbation solution may offer a more physically realizable description than the full exponential growth predicted by inviscid theories.

For BLT perturbations acting on the geostrophic base state, the response is diverse across horizontal versus vertical components and dissipation versus viscosity. Consistent with B19, we find that the horizontal component is predominantly frontolytic, whereas vertical viscosity drives frontogenesis. However, in contrast to Dauhajre et al. (2025), who identified a transition between frontolytic and frontogenetic regimes for vertical mixing depending on the Rossby–Ekman number combination, our perturbation analysis, assuming uniform viscosity and diffusivity, reveals that all relevant scenarios are frontogenetic. This difference highlights the sensitivity of the solution to the specific formulation of the turbulent fluxes and the base state. To maintain analytical tractability, we employ constant eddy diffusivity and viscosity, yet the formulation is robust enough to accommodate spatially inhomogeneous turbulent boundary layers in future extensions.

When finite-Rossby-number fronts and filaments are perturbed simultaneously by strain and BLT, vertical viscosity and diffusivity can attenuate strain-induced frontogenesis in certain parameter regimes, despite the inherent frontogenetic tendency of vertical viscosity. Critically, horizontal diffusivity acts as a potent stopper of frontogenesis and can counterbalance strain-induced sharpening when perturbation scales are comparable. Conversely, horizontal viscosity serves to accelerate frontal sharpening. Exploring the parameter space of Rossby, Ekman, and normalized strain numbers reveals outlier cases where BLT significantly modulates the strain impact. Specifically, in the vertical mixing scenario at the highest Rossby and Ekman numbers, turbulence generally enhances frontogenesis. However, at slightly lower but still order-unity Rossby numbers, this effect reverses, weakening the strain impact. At moderate Rossby and Ekman numbers, the interaction is variable, alternating between weakening and strengthening. This complex, non-monotonic interaction highlights the necessity of carefully characterizing both strain and BLT when parameterizing submesoscale dynamics (Zhang et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2026).

Our results also show broad consistency with recent Large Eddy Simulations (LES). For instance, Sullivan and McWilliams (2024) observed that boundary layer turbulence could arrest frontogenesis, a feature we capture analytically through the action of horizontal diffusivity. Furthermore, our asymptotic approach differs from and is complementary to other methods such as diagnostic force-balance decompositions or turbulent thermal wind (TTW) analyses (McWilliams, 2017; Crowe and Taylor, 2018). Diagnostic approaches, by their nature, do not capture the temporal evolution, while previous TTW analyses typically assume a small Rossby number. Our asymptotic framework is designed to illuminate different facets of the frontal dynamics. Our latest LES work explore comprehensive energetic interactions among submesoscale and BLT under spatially heterogeneous mesoscale forcing (Peng et al., 2026). The mesoscale field holds a range of strain effects, from strong convergence to divergence. The novelty of our approach here lies in decoupling these effects analytically to reveal their individual and competitive contributions across a wide parameter space. Therefore, in principle in can be applied to cases under negative strain (divergence), which is less explored but not uncommon in upper ocean multiscale dynamics.

The parameterized turbulent fluxes in our framework can, in principle, represent mixed-layer instability (MLI), which restratifies the mixed layer by releasing available potential energy from horizontal buoyancy gradients (Boccaletti et al., 2007). Recent analyses suggest that MLI exhibits characteristics of both baroclinic and barotropic instability (Kar et al., 2025). Our results can be extended to include a more detailed treatment of turbulent fluxes arising from both surface forcing (BLT) and submesoscale instabilities. This has significant implications for the development of coupled BLT-submesoscale parameterizations in ocean models.

The intricate evolution of the frontal tendency under combined strain and BLT forcing suggests that existing, simplified parameterization schemes may fail to capture key interactions in realistic, ageostrophic fronts and filaments. In particular, the spatial sensitivity of the BLT-induced frontal tendency to specific viscosity and diffusivity profiles is often underrepresented in mixed-layer parameterizations (Bodner et al., 2023, e.g.,). This underscores the critical need for revised parameterization frameworks that incorporate front-aware spatial variability to more accurately represent upper-ocean frontal evolution.

## Abstract

Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.

## 1. Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a powerful representation for static scene reconstruction and novel-view rendering, offering high visual fidelity and efficient rasterization (Kerbl et al., 2023). Building on this foundation, recent dynamic Gaussian methods extend Gaussian primitives across time through deformation, temporal conditioning, or explicit spacetime modeling, substantially advancing dynamic scene reconstruction and free-viewpoint rendering (Luiten et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024b). Among these developments, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as an effective representation for dynamic scene modeling, enabling high-fidelity rendering with strong efficiency (Wu et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024b). Together, these advances establish Gaussian splatting as a practical substrate for dynamic visual modeling.

At the same time, recent work has begun to study language grounding and semantic reasoning on Gaussian representations. In static 3D scenes, methods such as LangSplat (Qin et al., 2024), Gaussian Grouping (Ye et al., 2024), OpenGaussian (Wu et al., 2024a), Dr. Splat (Jun-Seong et al., 2025), Segment then Splat (Lu et al., 2025), and ReferSplat (He et al., 2025) connect Gaussian primitives with language or segmentation supervision. In dynamic settings, SA4D (Ji et al., 2024) and 4D LangSplat (Li et al., 2025) extend Gaussian-based semantics to time-varying scenes. However, many existing methods are optimized for category-level querying, scene-specific semantic fitting, or mask prediction, and are not designed for expressions involving temporal state changes, interaction cues, multi-target reasoning, or deliberately absent targets.

This gap becomes critical when the query involves temporal states, relations, or set-level constraints. A practical model should handle expressions such as the cookie broken into smaller pieces, the complete lemon before the cut, all objects except the hand and the metal cup, or descriptions with no valid referent. These queries require temporal reasoning, entity disambiguation, set-level constraints, and uncertainty-aware rejection. To address these limitations, we define Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), which requires a 4D Gaussian system to resolve complex natural-language referring expressions in dynamic scenes and produce temporally grounded, set-valued segmentation masks. Recognizing the lack of a benchmark for this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA (QA denotes Query Annotations), which evaluates three challenging categories: 4D-varying queries, multi-target or reasoning queries, and zero-target or distractor queries.

These observations reveal an abstraction gap between low-level Gaussian primitives and the entity-level units referred to by natural language. Dynamic Gaussian backbones provide efficient time-conditioned scene representations, but their primitives are not directly organized into persistent, language-addressable entities. Meanwhile, SA4D and 4D LangSplat enrich dynamic scenes with segmentation identities or learned language fields (Ji et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025), yet remain primarily oriented toward segmentation-centric outputs or scene-specific semantic fitting. Consequently, temporal-state composition, multi-entity selection, and zero-target rejection are not naturally supported within a unified referring protocol.

Motivated by this gap, we propose ReferGaussian, a training-free referring framework built upon 4DGS. Starting from a reconstructed 4D Gaussian scene, it uses mask-supported multi-view evidence to form persistent Gaussian entities, records their appearance, motion, relations, and valid temporal support in an EntityBank, and resolves structured referring constraints over this bank. MLLMs serve as the Refer-Planner for query decomposition and constraint extraction, while Grounded-SAM supplies 2D mask evidence. The final prediction is produced through explicit and inspectable entity-level selection, without scene-specific semantic training.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- (1) We formulate Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a novel task for language-grounded dynamic scene understanding involving temporal state changes, multi-target reasoning, and distractor rejection.

- (2) We establish R4D-Bench-QA, the first benchmark for R4DGS, featuring structured query annotations and pixel-level spatiotemporal supervision to address the current lack of evaluation standards.

- (3) We propose ReferGaussian, a training-free framework that organizes low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent entities addressable through language and performs constraint-aware 4D referring over an EntityBank.

## 2. Related Work

Dynamic Scene Reconstruction. NeRF (Mildenhall et al., 2020) and its dynamic variants (Park et al., 2021a; Pumarola et al., 2021; Park et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2021; Cao and Johnson, 2023) laid the foundation for neural dynamic view synthesis. 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) replaced volumetric rendering with explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives, making real-time rendering practical. Recent work extends Gaussian splatting to dynamic scenes through deformation, canonicalization, or explicit spacetime modeling, including Dynamic 3D Gaussians (Luiten et al., 2024), Deformable 3D Gaussians (Yang et al., 2024a), 4D Gaussian Splatting (Wu et al., 2024b), Real-time Photorealistic Dynamic Scene Representation and Rendering with 4D Gaussian Splatting (Yang et al., 2024b), and Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting (Li et al., 2024). These methods deliver strong rendering quality, yet their objective remains view synthesis. Our target is language-conditioned reasoning over dynamic entities. This requires temporal support that remains stable across rendering, downstream grouping, candidate ranking, and set-level decisions under ambiguous natural language. In practice, this difference is critical when multiple visually similar candidates coexist but only one satisfies temporal or relational constraints across a full event window.

Language-Grounded Semantic Reasoning. Visual semantic reasoning has advanced across various domains. In 2D video understanding, several works explore semantic tasks such as open-vocabulary and referring segmentation (Wu et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2023; Seo et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2026a; Jin et al., 2026b; Jin et al., 2026c). For static 3D scenes, current research explores two primary directions: open-vocabulary understanding and segmentation (Kerr et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024a; Jun-Seong et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026a; Ding et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Piekenbrinck et al., 2025), and referring expression grounding represented by ReferSplat (He et al., 2025). In dynamic contexts, while SA4D (Ji et al., 2024) and 4D LangSplat (Li et al., 2025) enable time-sensitive language querying, they primarily focus on semantic segmentation, with limited coverage of complex referring understanding. To our knowledge, referring grounding in dynamic Gaussian scenes has not been systematically formulated or evaluated. Unlike existing methods that rely on scene-specific semantic retraining or learned language fields, ReferGaussian resolves referents through entity-level matching within a query-reusable structure. This training-free design supports robust reasoning over temporal states and set-valued targets through persistent entity records and explicit constraints.

Foundation Models. Large vision-language and segmentation foundation models provide strong building blocks for language-grounded scene reasoning. Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025a) supports structured interpretation of natural-language expressions, while Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2024b), Segment Anything (Kirillov et al., 2023), and Grounded-SAM (Ren et al., 2024) enable text-conditioned mask extraction. Recent multimodal systems (Liu et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2024) further improve prompt following and visual grounding. ReferGaussian uses these models as modular components for query parsing and visual evidence extraction within a structured entity-centric pipeline. This decomposition improves diagnostic ability: query decomposition errors, mask evidence errors, and entity association errors can be analyzed separately.

## 3. Task and Benchmark

In this section, we first formalize Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS) and clarify its task setting. We then introduce R4D-Bench-QA, our benchmark for dynamic 4D referring understanding, together with its construction pipeline, annotation protocol, query taxonomy, and evaluation metrics.

### 3.1. Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS)

Given a multi-view dynamic video, a precomputed 4D Gaussian scene representation, and a natural-language query $q$ , R4DGS identifies the referred entities and produces their frame-aligned segmentation masks. The referent may be a single entity, multiple entities, or an empty set, depending on the spatiotemporal, relational, and set-level constraints expressed by the query.

R4DGS adds three requirements to conventional referring: (1) Temporally varying queries specify an event stage or a state before or after a transition. (2) Set-valued and reasoning-intensive queries express conjunction, exclusion, quantification, or relations among entities. (3) Zero-target and distractor queries may describe no valid referent and therefore return an empty prediction.

### 3.2. R4D-Bench-QA

To evaluate R4DGS systematically, we construct R4D-Bench-QA, a query-annotation benchmark with deliberate coverage of three query categories and pixel-level spatiotemporal annotations. Its 12 scenes come from two dynamic-scene sources: six HyperNeRF (Park et al., 2021b) scenes provide 47 queries, and six Neu3D (Li et al., 2022) scenes provide 42 queries, for 89 densely annotated sentence-level queries in total. Table 1 compares R4D-Bench-QA with representative datasets used by Gaussian-language methods. Existing resources are either limited to static 2D/3D scenes or primarily designed for open-vocabulary segmentation, with limited support for sentence-level dynamic referring. R4D-Bench-QA jointly supports dynamic scenes, sentence-level referring, time-varying semantics, temporal constraints, and spatial grounding.

Benchmark Construction. As illustrated in Figure 3, the benchmark is constructed in three stages. In Stage 1, each dynamic video is processed to obtain temporally associated mask tracks and a vocabulary of trackable object candidates. Segmentation models provide frame-level mask evidence, while an MLLM assists in identifying concise object phrases that remain visually traceable throughout the sequence.

In Stage 2, annotators inspect the mask overlays and divide each sequence into semantically meaningful temporal segments according to object-state changes, interactions, and event boundaries. Key frames are selected from each segment to summarize its visual content. Based on the tracked objects and temporal segments, annotators construct entity-centric referring expressions and associate each expression with its complete target set, valid temporal support, and frame-aligned masks. Multi-target annotations include the complete set of entities satisfying the query.

Stage 3 performs query-specific quality control. Temporally varying queries are checked for unambiguous state descriptions and valid event boundaries. Multi-target queries are checked for relational consistency and completeness of the annotated target set. Zero-target queries are retained only when no annotated entity satisfies all query constraints. Three expert annotators perform verification, while MLLM-based checks flag ambiguous or inconsistent cases for human inspection.

Together, they span state transitions, temporal ordering, conjunction, disjunction, exclusion, object interactions, and target-cardinality constraints. Annotation Representation. For each query $q$ , the annotation contains the relevant frame set $\mathcal{F}_{q}$ , the target entities, and a binary ground-truth mask $M^{*}_{q,t}$ for every evaluated frame $t\in\mathcal{F}_{q}$ . For a multi-target query, $M^{*}_{q,t}$ is the frame-wise union of the masks of all valid target entities. A zero-target query has $M^{*}_{q,t}=\varnothing$ for all evaluated frames. Predictions are represented analogously by $\hat{M}_{q,t}$ , obtained by rasterizing the selected Gaussian entities.

### 3.3. Evaluation Metrics

We adopt the time-sensitive protocol of 4D LangSplat (Li et al., 2025). It evaluates temporal target activation and spatial mask quality, with Acc denoting frame-wise temporal activation accuracy. Let the ground-truth and predicted active-frame sets be $\mathcal{T}^{*}_{q}=\{t\in\mathcal{F}_{q}:|M^{*}_{q,t}|>0\}$ and $\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{q}=\{t\in\mathcal{F}_{q}:|\hat{M}_{q,t}|>0\}$ .

Temporal Accuracy. The temporal accuracy of query $q$ is

$$ \operatorname{Acc}(q)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}_{q}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{F}_{q}}\mathbb{1}\!\left[\mathbb{1}[t\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{q}]=\mathbb{1}[t\in\mathcal{T}^{*}_{q}]\right]. $$

This metric penalizes both missed valid intervals and false activations outside the annotated temporal support.

Video IoU. Following the same protocol, video IoU is

$$ \operatorname{vIoU}(q)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{q}\cup\mathcal{T}^{*}_{q}|}\sum_{t\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{q}\cap\mathcal{T}^{*}_{q}}\frac{|\hat{M}_{q,t}\cap M^{*}_{q,t}|}{|\hat{M}_{q,t}\cup M^{*}_{q,t}|},&|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{q}\cup\mathcal{T}^{*}_{q}|>0,\\[8.0pt]
1,&|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{q}\cup\mathcal{T}^{*}_{q}|=0.\end{cases} $$

Frames outside the temporal intersection contribute zero, so vIoU penalizes temporal errors, false targets, and inaccurate mask boundaries. For a valid zero-target query, vIoU is one only when the prediction remains empty. ZeroAcc is the percentage of zero-target queries with empty predictions throughout the evaluated frames. Incomplete or unresolved outputs count as failures.

The reported Acc and vIoU average their query-level scores:

$$ \operatorname{Acc}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\operatorname{Acc}(q),\quad\operatorname{vIoU}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\operatorname{vIoU}(q). $$

For multi-target queries, evaluation uses the frame-wise union of all selected and annotated target masks.

We also report Acc and vIoU for each of the three query categories separately on HyperNeRF and Neu3D. These six source-category slices expose whether a model’s behavior is consistent across both scene sources and all query types; Figure 7 visualizes this breakdown for the planner analysis.

## 4. Method

ReferGaussian addresses the abstraction gap between low-level dynamic Gaussian primitives and the entity-level units referred to by natural language. Given a precomputed 4D Gaussian scene, our method constructs persistent Gaussian entities from multi-frame visual evidence, organizes them into an EntityBank, and performs constraint-aware referent selection without optimizing an additional scene-specific semantic field.

### 4.1. Preliminaries

3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting represents a scene with a collection of anisotropic Gaussians $g_{i}=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{s}_{i},\mathbf{c}_{i},\alpha_{i})$ , where $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}$ is the center, $\mathbf{r}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{s}_{i}$ parameterize rotation and scale, and $\mathbf{c}_{i}$ and $\alpha_{i}$ denote color and opacity, respectively (Kerbl et al., 2023). The covariance is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}=\mathbf{R}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{i}^{\top}$ , where $\mathbf{R}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{i}$ are constructed from $\mathbf{r}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{s}_{i}$ . After projection, the color at pixel $\mathbf{p}$ is alpha-composited in depth order:

$$ \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{p})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_{i}(\mathbf{p})\alpha_{i}(\mathbf{p})\mathbf{c}_{i},\qquad T_{i}(\mathbf{p})=\prod_{j<i}\left(1-\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{p})\right). $$

4D Gaussian Splatting. Dynamic Gaussian methods condition Gaussian primitives on time. A common formulation predicts position, rotation, and scale offsets with a temporal deformation function $\mathcal{D}_{\theta}$ (Wu et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024a):

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\theta}(g_{i},t) \displaystyle=(\Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}^{t},\Delta\mathbf{r}_{i}^{t},\Delta\mathbf{s}_{i}^{t}), \displaystyle(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}^{t},\mathbf{r}_{i}^{t},\mathbf{s}_{i}^{t}) \displaystyle=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{s}_{i})+\mathcal{D}_{\theta}(g_{i},t). $$

Equation (4) then applies to the time-conditioned primitives. In this work, the reconstructed 4D Gaussian scene is provided as input, and our contribution begins with organizing its primitives for referring understanding.

R4DGS uses explicit referential units that support joint temporal, relational, cardinality, exclusion, and empty-target constraints.

### 4.2. Framework

Given dynamic Gaussians $\mathcal{G}$ , calibrated video frames $\{\mathbf{I}_{t}\}$ , and a query $q$ , ReferGaussian follows three semantic stages.

Stage 1: query-guided entity discovery uses an MLLM-based Refer-Planner to extract trackable subject phrases and coarse temporal cues. Grounded-SAM2 produces phrase-conditioned mask tracks, which are iteratively lifted from sampled frames into Gaussian-supported candidate entities.

Stage 2: EntityBank construction summarizes each candidate using representative observations, active temporal segments, appearance and state descriptions, motion cues, and relations. These records form an inspectable EntityBank over the reconstructed scene.

Stage 3: constraint-aware referent selection validates the structured query and selects candidate entities and temporal segments under identity, temporal, relational, cardinality, exclusion, and zero-target constraints. The selected Gaussian supports are finally rasterized to produce frame-aligned masks.

Figure 5 illustrates the overall pipeline. This decomposition changes the reasoning unit from a pixel or frame-wise feature match to an entity with persistent Gaussian support. Stage 1 establishes spatial and temporal correspondence between 2D evidence and 4D primitives, Stage 2 makes the entities language-addressable, and Stage 3 produces a globally consistent set-valued answer.

### 4.3. Mask-Supported Persistent Entity Construction

For a subject phrase produced by the Refer-Planner, let $\mathbf{M}_{t}$ be its tracked mask and $\Pi_{t}(g_{i})$ the projected footprint of Gaussian $g_{i}$ . We aggregate mask agreement over sampled frames with one score:

$$ S_{i}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}u_{i}^{t}\frac{|\Pi_{t}(g_{i})\cap\mathbf{M}_{t}|}{|\Pi_{t}(g_{i})|+\epsilon}}{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}u_{i}^{t}+\epsilon}. $$

Here, $u_{i}^{t}$ is a projection-validity indicator. It is active when the Gaussian has positive depth, its projected center lies inside the image, and its rasterized footprint contributes alpha mass. This definition follows the visibility checks used by the 4DGS renderer.

Algorithm 1 iteratively updates a support-ranked candidate and validates it by rendering its mask back to the sampled frames. Each round uses six active frames, or all active frames when fewer are available. We run at most ten rounds, stop when mean render-back IoU reaches $0.70$ , and also stop after three validation rounds without improvement. The best validated candidate is retained.

The selected Gaussian set becomes a candidate entity $e_{m}$ with support $\mathcal{G}_{m}$ . The resulting entity represents a physical candidate together with one or more temporally valid states.

### 4.4. EntityBank Construction and Constraint-Aware Querying

In Stage 2, each candidate is stored as

$$ e_{m}=\bigl(\mathrm{id}_{m},\mathcal{G}_{m},\mathcal{T}_{m},\mathcal{X}_{m},\mathcal{A}_{m},\mathcal{R}_{m}\bigr), $$

where $\mathcal{G}_{m}$ is its Gaussian support, $\mathcal{T}_{m}$ contains candidate active segments, $\mathcal{X}_{m}$ contains representative crops and track summaries, and $\mathcal{A}_{m}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{m}$ contain appearance or state attributes and inter-entity relations. The collection $\mathcal{B}=\{e_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}$ forms EntityBank. Constructed entity records and visual evidence are cached and reused when subsequent queries involve the same tracked objects.

The MLLM-based Refer-Planner converts each query into a schema containing trackable subject phrases, identity and state attributes, relational and exclusion constraints, temporal predicates, optional target cardinality, and an explicit zero-target flag. Schema validation rejects malformed outputs, unknown EntityBank identifiers, and incomplete fields, then requests a corrected plan.

In Stage 3, the Refer-Planner performs closed-set selection over the identifiers and temporal segments supplied by EntityBank. It jointly checks identity, temporal, relational, cardinality, and exclusion constraints, so every prediction remains grounded in supported candidates. An explicitly absent target, or the absence of any candidate set satisfying all constraints, produces an empty selection. The selected Gaussian supports are rasterized only within their chosen temporal segments, and masks from multiple selected entities are combined frame by frame. This yields the final spatiotemporal segmentation while keeping the query interpretation, entity evidence, and referent decision inspectable.

Under mask perturbations, erosion, dilation, and proposal dropping retain $32.1$ – $33.9$ vIoU, remaining within $2.3$ points of the original masks. Merge and split errors fall to $19.4$ and $22.7$ because they change entity identity and propagate to later constraints. The contrast separates tolerance to local mask noise from sensitivity to incorrect entity composition.

Efficiency and reuse. EntityBank reuse cuts runtime from about $600$ to $200$ seconds and local MLLM calls from six to three (Figure 8) using local inference. The initial query is dominated by mask detection and entity construction, while cached queries reuse tracks, visual evidence, and entity descriptions. The remaining work is concentrated in query planning, semantic assignment, selection, and final rendering.

Failure modes. Remaining failures involve crowded contact events, ambiguous long queries, breakage, and severe occlusion. These cases combine rapid topology changes and uncertain identity boundaries, motivating stronger temporal association and calibrated uncertainty.

## 6. Conclusion

We formulated Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a new task for grounding complex natural-language expressions in dynamic Gaussian scenes, and introduced R4D-Bench-QA to evaluate temporal-state, multi-target, and zero-target referring. We further presented ReferGaussian, a training-free Gaussian-to-Entity framework that organizes dynamic Gaussian primitives into persistent, language-addressable entities and performs constraint-aware referent selection through EntityBank. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate the effectiveness of entity-level reasoning for complex spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Together, R4DGS, R4D-Bench-QA, and ReferGaussian establish a foundation for language-guided interaction and structured reasoning over dynamic 4D scene representations.
